faq.hydrationA: Dough hydration is the ratio of water to flour in a bread dough, expressed as a percentage. It's calculated as (water weight / flour weight) x 100. For example, 500g flour and 350g water gives 70% hydration. Hydration is one of the most important factors determining your bread's texture, crumb structure, and crust.
faq.yeastQ: How do I convert between different types of yeast?
faq.yeastA: The standard conversion ratios are: fresh yeast to active dry yeast = 3:1, and fresh yeast to instant yeast = 3:1. Active dry and instant yeast are generally interchangeable 1:1 in modern baking. Our yeast converter handles all three types automatically.
faq.bakersA: Baker's percentage is a notation system where every ingredient is expressed as a percentage of the total flour weight. Flour is always 100%. If a recipe calls for 70% water, 2% salt, and 1% yeast, that means for every 1000g of flour, you use 700g water, 20g salt, and 10g yeast. This system makes recipes infinitely scalable and easy to compare.
faq.pizzaQ: How much dough do I need per pizza?
faq.pizzaA: The amount of dough per pizza depends on the size and style. For a 12-inch (30cm) pizza: Neapolitan needs about 250g, New York style about 320g, and Sicilian about 450g. Our pizza dough calculator figures this out automatically based on your pizza size and style.
faq.freeA: Yes, completely free. No sign-up, no ads, no tracking. We built BreadRatio because we love baking and wanted a simple tool that just works. All calculations happen right in your browser — we never see your data.
faq.starterQ: How do I maintain a sourdough starter?
faq.starterA: Keep your starter at room temperature and feed it every 12-24 hours using a ratio of 1:1:1 (starter:flour:water by weight). Discard all but 20-50g before each feeding to keep the quantity manageable. For less frequent baking, store in the refrigerator and feed once weekly — our starter calculator handles both daily and target-amount feeding plans.
faq.scalerQ: Can I scale baking recipes linearly?
faq.scalerA: Yes, ingredients scale linearly — double the flour means double everything else. However, fermentation time, mixing time, and baking time don't always scale perfectly. Our recipe scaler handles the ingredient math instantly, and the FAQ on that page explains the practical timing adjustments for scaled batches.

hydration.faq1A: Dough hydration is the ratio of water weight to flour weight, expressed as a percentage. Formula: Hydration % = (Water g / Flour g) x 100. It is the single most important factor determining your bread's texture, crumb structure, and crust.
hydration.faq2Q: What hydration is best for sourdough?
hydration.faq2A: Most sourdough recipes use 65-75% hydration. Beginners should start at 65-68% for easier handling. Experienced bakers often go to 75-80% for a more open crumb.
hydration.faq3Q: How does hydration affect bread texture?
hydration.faq3A: Higher hydration = more open crumb, thinner crust, more extensible dough. Lower hydration = tighter crumb, thicker crust, easier to shape.
hydration.faq4Q: How do I adjust hydration for different flours?
hydration.faq4A: Whole wheat and rye flours absorb significantly more water than white bread flour. A recipe using 70% hydration with all-purpose flour may need 75-80% when using 50% whole wheat. Always add water gradually — flour absorption varies by brand, batch, and humidity.
hydration.faq5Q: What happens if my dough is too wet or too dry?
hydration.faq5A: Too wet: dough spreads flat, difficult to shape, sticky and unmanageable. Fix by adding flour 5-10g at a time during kneading. Too dry: dough is stiff, tears easily, produces dense bread. Fix by adding water 5-10g at a time and mixing thoroughly.
hydration.faq6Q: What hydration levels match different bread types?
hydration.faq6A: 50-57% — Bagels, pretzels (very stiff). 58-65% — Sandwich bread, rolls (soft, fine crumb). 66-70% — Country loaves, everyday sourdough (balanced). 71-78% — Artisan sourdough, rustic loaves (open crumb). 79-85% — Ciabatta, focaccia (very open). 85%+ — Pan de cristal.

scaler.faq1Q: How does the recipe scaler work?
scaler.faq1A: Enter your original recipe's yield (e.g., makes 2 loaves) and the target yield (e.g., want 5 loaves). The calculator computes the scaling factor and multiplies every ingredient by that ratio. All calculations preserve the exact proportions of your original recipe, so your bread turns out the same — just in a different quantity.
scaler.faq2Q: Can I scale between different units (loaves to grams)?
scaler.faq2A: The scaler works with any consistent unit. If your original recipe yields 800g of dough and you want 2000g, enter 800 and 2000. If you use 'loaves', both yields must be in loaves. The key is using the same unit for both original and target yield.
scaler.faq3Q: What if my scaled amounts end up with weird decimals?
scaler.faq3A: The calculator rounds to reasonable precision (one decimal place). For home baking, ±1g difference won't affect your results. If you get 2.3g of something small like yeast, use 2g — the difference is negligible. For large batches, round to the nearest gram.
scaler.faq4A: Yes, but timing doesn't scale linearly. Doubling a sourdough recipe doubles ingredients but the fermentation time stays roughly the same if the dough temperature and starter percentage are unchanged. A larger dough mass may ferment slightly faster because it retains heat better.
scaler.faq5Q: Does scaling affect baking time and temperature?
scaler.faq5A: Baking temperature stays the same regardless of batch size. Baking time may need minor adjustments: larger loaves need slightly longer (add 5-10 minutes), while dividing into the same loaf size as the original means no time change at all.
scaler.faq6Q: What's the best scaling approach for very large batches?
scaler.faq6A: For batches above 5x original: 1) Mix in stages if your mixer can't handle the full volume. 2) Monitor dough temperature — large masses generate more friction heat during mixing. 3) Consider dividing dough before bulk fermentation if your containers aren't large enough. 4) Use weight measurements (grams), never volume (cups), for accuracy at scale.

yeast.subtitle: Convert between fresh yeast, active dry yeast, and instant yeast. Standard conversion ratios built in — no guesswork needed.
yeast.faq1Q: How do I convert fresh yeast to dry yeast?
yeast.faq1A: Divide the fresh yeast amount by 3. For example, 30g fresh yeast = 10g active dry or instant yeast. The standard ratio is 3:1 (fresh:dry).
yeast.faq2Q: Is active dry yeast the same as instant yeast?
yeast.faq2A: They are interchangeable 1:1 in most recipes. The main difference is how you use them: active dry yeast should be dissolved in warm water first (bloomed), while instant yeast can be mixed directly with dry ingredients.
yeast.faq3Q: Can I substitute instant yeast for fresh yeast in sourdough?
yeast.faq3A: Yes. If a recipe calls for fresh yeast and you only have instant, use 1/3 of the amount. However, note that sourdough traditionally relies on natural leavening from a starter.
yeast.faq4Q: How can I tell if my yeast is still active?
yeast.faq4A: Proof it: dissolve 1 tsp sugar in 1/4 cup warm water (38-43°C / 100-110°F), sprinkle yeast on top. After 5-10 minutes, it should foam and bubble vigorously. No foam = dead yeast. Active dry yeast needs this step; instant yeast doesn't but can still be tested this way.
yeast.faq5Q: Does yeast type affect rising time?
yeast.faq5A: Yes. Instant yeast works fastest, active dry is slightly slower and benefits from blooming first, fresh yeast is slowest but adds subtle flavor complexity. For the same amount, instant yeast may cut rising time by 15-25% compared to active dry. Temperature is the bigger factor — every 8°C increase roughly doubles yeast activity rate.
yeast.faq6Q: Can I use less yeast and ferment longer?
yeast.faq6A: Absolutely — and many artisan bakers prefer this. Using 25-50% of the called-for yeast and extending fermentation (overnight in the fridge) develops more complex flavors, better gluten structure, and improved digestibility. Our calculator gives a standard 0.5-1% yeast ratio; you can safely halve it for a slow, cold ferment.

bakers.subtitle: Calculate baker's percentages — the professional standard for bread formulas. Flour is always 100%. Every other ingredient is expressed relative to total flour weight.
bakers.addFlour: Add an ingredient with "flour" in its name as the 100% reference.
bakers.faq1A: Baker's percentage is a notation system where every ingredient in a recipe is expressed as a percentage of the total flour weight. Flour is always 100%. This system makes recipes infinitely scalable and easy to compare across different formulas.
bakers.faq2Q: Why use baker's percentage instead of regular percentages?
bakers.faq2A: Regular percentages add up to 100% of the total. Baker's percentages don't — they reference flour alone. This is more useful because it tells you the ratio of each ingredient to flour at a glance.
bakers.faq3Q: What's a typical baker's percentage for a sourdough loaf?
bakers.faq3A: A typical sourdough formula: Flour 100%, Water 70-78%, Salt 2%, Starter/Levain 20%. This gives you a 70-78% hydration dough.
bakers.faq4Q: How do I convert a regular recipe to baker's percentage?
bakers.faq4A: 1) Identify the total flour weight (combine all flour types). 2) Divide each ingredient weight by total flour weight. 3) Multiply by 100. Example: 500g flour, 350g water, 10g salt → Water: 350/500×100 = 70%, Salt: 10/500×100 = 2%. That's it — flour is always 100%.
bakers.faq5Q: How do I handle recipes with multiple types of flour?
bakers.faq5A: Add all flour weights together for the 100% reference. If a recipe has 400g bread flour + 100g whole wheat = 500g total flour, that 500g is your 100%. Then calculate each ingredient's percentage against 500g. Each flour type is expressed as its own percentage: bread flour 80%, whole wheat 20%.
bakers.faq6Q: What are common baker's percentages for different breads?
bakers.faq6A: Baguette: Flour 100%, Water 70-76%, Salt 2%, Yeast 0.5-1%. Brioche: Flour 100%, Butter 40-50%, Eggs 20-30%, Sugar 10-15%, Yeast 2-3%. Ciabatta: Flour 100%, Water 75-82%, Salt 2%, Yeast 0.5%, Olive oil 2-3%. Enriched sandwich bread: Flour 100%, Water 55-65%, Butter 5-10%, Sugar 5-8%, Milk powder 4-6%, Yeast 1.5%.

pizza.faq2Q: What hydration is best for pizza dough?
pizza.faq2A: Neapolitan: 60-65%. New York: 62-65%. Sicilian/Detroit: 70-75%. Thin & Crispy: 55-60%.
pizza.faq3Q: How much yeast for pizza dough?
pizza.faq3A: This calculator uses 0.5% instant yeast (baker's percentage). For a 300g flour pizza dough, that's about 1.5g of instant yeast. For a slow 24-72 hour cold ferment, you can reduce to 0.2-0.3%.
pizza.faq4Q: Should I cold-ferment or room-temperature proof my pizza dough?
pizza.faq4A: Cold fermentation (24-72 hours at 4°C) is the gold standard for flavor and texture — it slows yeast activity while enzymes continue breaking down starches into sugars, creating complex flavors and better browning. Room-temperature proofing (2-4 hours) works for same-day pizza but won't develop the same depth. For best results: mix, bulk ferment 1 hour at room temp, ball, then refrigerate 24-48 hours.
pizza.faq5Q: What flour is best for pizza dough?
pizza.faq5A: High-protein bread flour (12-14% protein) gives the best chewy, structured crust. Tipo 00 flour is traditional for Neapolitan pizza — finely milled, about 12.5% protein, ideal for high-heat ovens. All-purpose flour works but produces a softer, less chewy crust. Avoid cake or pastry flour for pizza.
pizza.faq6Q: Why does my pizza dough shrink when I stretch it?
pizza.faq6A: Dough that snaps back aggressively hasn't relaxed enough. Gluten tightens during handling. Solutions: 1) Let the dough rest at room temperature for 30-60 minutes after balling before stretching. 2) Use a well-rested dough — cold dough fights you more. 3) Stretch gently from the center outward, letting gravity help. 4) Don't over-knead initially — excessive gluten development makes stretching harder.
pizza.faq7A: Yes, pizza dough freezes excellently. After the first rise, portion into balls, lightly oil, wrap tightly in plastic wrap, and freeze for up to 3 months. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator, then let come to room temperature (1-2 hours) before stretching. The cold ferment during thawing actually improves flavor.

starter.faq1Q: What is a sourdough starter feeding ratio?
starter.faq1A: A feeding ratio tells you how much starter, flour, and water to combine at each feeding. Written as S:F:W (starter:flour:water), a 1:1:1 ratio means equal parts of each.
starter.faq2Q: How much starter should I keep vs discard?
starter.faq2A: It depends on your baking schedule. For daily feedings with a 1:1:1 ratio, keeping 20–50g is common to avoid waste.
starter.faq3Q: What hydration should my starter be?
starter.faq3A: Most bakers maintain their starter at 100% hydration, meaning equal parts flour and water by weight.
starter.faq4Q: How often should I feed my starter?
starter.faq4A: If kept at room temperature (20–24°C), feed your starter every 12–24 hours using a 1:1:1 ratio. In warmer climates it may need feeding every 8–12 hours.
starter.faq5Q: How do I know when my starter is ready to use?
starter.faq5A: A ripe starter doubles or triples in volume within 4-6 hours of feeding, has a domed top (not sunken), smells pleasantly sour and yeasty (not like nail polish remover), and passes the float test: a spoonful dropped in water floats. If it peaks and collapses before you use it, feed again.
starter.faq6Q: What is the dark liquid on top of my starter (hooch)?
starter.faq6A: Hooch is a harmless alcohol byproduct that forms when your starter is hungry — it means the yeast has consumed all available food. Pour it off or stir it back in (it adds sourness). Hooch signals you need to feed more frequently or use a higher feeding ratio. A healthy starter should not develop hooch between regular 12-24 hour feedings.
starter.faq7Q: Can I revive a neglected starter?
starter.faq7A: Almost always yes. Discard all but a tablespoon of starter, feed at 1:2:2 ratio twice daily for 3-4 days at warm room temperature (24-26°C). Even if it smells terrible or has separated, the microorganisms are resilient. Consistent feeding with fresh flour and water almost always revives a starter within a week.
